claim: AI coding assistants speed up only the coding stage of the SDLC; because review and testing were already the slower stages, assistant adoption alone pushes the bottleneck downstream to PR review and on-call rather than shortening end-to-end delivery.
stance_target: pillar 5: triggers, infrastructure, continuous operation — need for whole-pipeline automation, not point tools
scope_conditions: enterprise engineering orgs adopting AI coding assistants, 2026
quoted_support: Almost every org has rolled out AI coding assistants; far fewer ship faster, because an assistant speeds up only the coding stage, and coding was rarely the slow part.

claim: An AI software factory requires a governed registry of every agent and what it can touch, scoped context, cost tied to work delivered, and permissions with a full audit trail — retrofitting this after agents are already in production is far harder than scoping it from the start.
quoted_support: A factory gives governance one place to live: a registry of every agent and what it can touch, scoped context, cost tied to work delivered, and permissions with a full audit trail... We caution against letting it form by accident; retrofitting governance onto hundreds of agents already in production is far harder than scoping it in from the start.

claim: Measuring AI software factory ROI should track delivery metrics (lead time, deployment frequency, change failure rate), autonomy share (% incidents/PRs resolved end-to-end by agents), and governance/cost metrics (policy violations caught, blast radius of agent actions, cost per unit of work) — explicitly NOT token spend or percent of code written by AI, which are vanity metrics.
stance_target: pillar 6: cost & resource optimization — correct metrics to optimize for
quoted_support: Do not optimize for token spend or share of code written by AI; those measure activity, not outcome... we anchor measurement to throughput, safety, and cost per unit of work shipped.

claim: Three recommended starter workflows for an AI software factory are incident response, ticket/bug resolution, and security remediation, chosen because output is verifiable, risk is limited, and mistakes are cheap to undo.
stance_target: pillar 5: phased rollout of continuous-operation agentic workflows
quoted_support: Run one line end to end, starting where output is verifiable, risk is limited, and mistakes are cheap to undo. The teams that succeed here resist automating everything at once, and prove one line works before extending the pattern.

claim: 'Dark software factory' (lights-off engineering, code ships that no human has read) is the endpoint of AI-led engineering but is not expected or desirable for most teams in the near term; a human should remain in the loop for anything touching money, data, or safety.
stance_target: limits of full autonomy / appropriate human oversight boundary
scope_conditions: AI-led SDLC endpoint framing, traces to Bob Bemer's 1968 economics-of-program-production paper
quoted_support: As Google engineer Addy Osmani puts it, it is where 'code ships that no human has read.' ... We do not expect most teams to run fully dark soon, nor to want to.

claim: CI/CD pipeline reliability is a prerequisite milestone before handing any SDLC stage to an agent — agents can only run a stage of the line as far as that pipeline is automated and trustworthy.
stance_target: pillar 5: infrastructure prerequisites for continuous agentic operation
quoted_support: Agents run the line only as far as that pipeline is automated and trustworthy, so fix flaky tests or manual deploy steps before handing any stage to an agent.
